title: Recognising Functions, Loops and Branches
summary: Disassemblers find most functions automatically, but understanding a function means recognising its parts: where it starts and ends, what its arguments and result are, and how its control flow maps to `if`, loops and `switch`. This lesson turns chapter 7's patterns into a reading routine for unknown functions, and covers the cases where automatic analysis gets function boundaries wrong.
markdown:
## Where functions start and end A disassembler finds functions by following calls from known starting points (the entry point, exports, the `.pdata` unwind table from lesson 8.02, which lists most functions' start and end RVAs on x64). Signs of a function start: - it is the target of `call` instructions; - it begins with a typical **prologue**: saving non-volatile registers (`push rbx`, `mov [rsp+8], rbx`), `sub rsp, N`; - it is listed in `.pdata`; - it follows padding bytes (`CC` or `90`) after the previous function's `ret`. Signs of an end: `ret` after an epilogue, or a `jmp` to another function (a tail call, lesson 7.11). Automatic analysis goes wrong when code is only reached through pointers (a vtable, a callback table, a jump table it did not decode), or when data sits in a code section. Ghidra then shows bytes that are not disassembled; pressing `D` (disassemble) and `F` (create function) at a likely start fixes it. ## A reading routine For each unknown function: 1. **Signature first.** Which of `rcx`, `rdx`, `r8`, `r9`, `xmm0` to `xmm3` are read before being written? Those are the arguments (lesson 7.06). Is `rax`/`eax`/`xmm0` set just before every `ret`? That is a result. `eax` set but only `al` used by callers suggests a `bool`. 2. **Calls next.** Which functions does it call, and are any of them imports (named for you) or functions you already named? Calls often explain more than everything else together. 3. **Constants and strings.** Format strings, error messages, magic numbers (`0x5A4D` is "MZ"; `0x3F800000` is 1.0f). 4. **Control flow.** Draw or view the graph: loops are back edges, decisions are diamonds, `switch` is a jump table (lesson 7.07). 5. **Memory accesses.** Offsets from argument registers are struct members (lesson 7.08). 6. **Name it**, even provisionally ("probably_load_config"), and move on. Refine later. ## Loops in the graph A loop shows up in a function graph as an arrow going **back up** to a block that dominates it (one that every path into the loop passes through). Its parts: ```mermaid flowchart TB G["guard: count == 0?"] -->|"no"| B["loop body
(the block the back edge targets)"] G -->|"yes"| X["after the loop"] B --> T["increment, compare"] T -->|"back edge: go round again"| B T -->|"done"| X ``` Recognising the **induction variable** (the register incremented each time round and compared against a limit) tells you what the loop iterates over; the memory accesses that use it tell you the array and its element size. The practice task finds loops from a list of jumps, the first step automatic tools perform. ## Branches that are not ifs Not every conditional jump is an `if` in the source: | Pattern | Source | |---|---| | A compare and jump straight after a call, to an error path | `if (!ok) return error;` or an exception-free error check | | `test rax, rax` / `je` after a call returning a pointer | A null check | | A jump to a block that calls a function with a string like "Assertion failed" | An assert | | `cmp` against a value, then a call to a function that never returns (`abort`, a throw helper) | A bounds check or failed precondition | | Several jumps to one block that sets the same return value | Early returns merged by the compiler | ## When there are no symbols for library code Functions from the C and C++ runtime are compiled into your program. Without a PDB, they look like any other unknown function. Ghidra's **Function ID** analyser recognises many by their bytes, and recognising the common ones by behaviour saves a lot of time: `memcpy`/`memset` (byte loops or `rep movsb`/`rep stosb`), `strlen` (a loop looking for a zero byte), `operator new` (calls `malloc`, throws on failure), `std::string` constructors (lesson 2.08's small buffer: compares a length with 15). ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Assuming the disassembler found every function > Code reached only through pointers may be missing. Look for undisassembled bytes in code sections. > [!warning] Reading every register as an argument > Only registers read before being written in the function's first block are arguments. > [!warning] Spending hours inside runtime library code > Recognise it, name it, and move on to the program's own logic. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What are signs that an address is the start of a function? - It is a multiple of 4,096 - It holds the bytes `00 00 00 00` + Calls target it, it has a prologue, or `.pdata` lists it - It is the first address of the `.data` section > Several of these signs together make it almost certain. ? What is an induction variable? - A variable that holds a function's return value + The variable that changes by a fixed step each time round a loop and is compared with the limit - A variable the compiler created that has no name in the source - A pointer used to call a virtual function > It shows what the loop iterates over, such as an index into an array. ? What is the most useful first step when reading an unknown function? - Read every instruction in order from the top - Rename every register - Look for the longest loop + Work out its arguments, its return value and its calls > Arguments and calls frame everything else in the function. ? How can you tell which registers are a function's arguments? - They are the registers used most in the function - They are always all four + Argument registers that are read before being written > Unused argument registers are simply never read. ? What marks a loop in a function graph? + A back edge to an earlier block - Any conditional jump at all - A call instruction in a block > The target of the back edge is the loop's head. ? `test rax, rax` / `je error` straight after a call. What is it probably? - A loop over the result + A null check of the result - A switch on the result > Functions returning pointers use null to signal failure. ```
ideas:
- In Ghidra, open the Function Graph of a function with a loop and identify the guard, the body and the back edge.
- Find a function in your target that Ghidra did not name, and work out its signature using the routine above before reading the decompiler.
- Look for `memset` and `memcpy` in a Release build of the lesson 9.04 target.

cards.q: What are signs that an address is the start of a function?
cards.a:
Calls target it, it has a prologue, or `.pdata` lists it

Several of these signs together make it almost certain.

The variable that changes by a fixed step each time round a loop and is compared with the limit

It shows what the loop iterates over, such as an index into an array.

cards.q: What is the most useful first step when reading an unknown function?
cards.a:
Work out its arguments, its return value and its calls

Arguments and calls frame everything else in the function.

cards.q: How can you tell which registers are a function's arguments?
cards.a:
Argument registers that are read before being written

Unused argument registers are simply never read.

cards.q: What marks a loop in a function graph?
cards.a:
A back edge to an earlier block

The target of the back edge is the loop's head.

cards.q: `test rax, rax` / `je error` straight after a call. What is it probably?
cards.a:
A null check of the result

Functions returning pointers use null to signal failure.
